Meister Eckhart
mīs´tẽr ĕk´härt
n. (Meister Eckhart, c. 1260–c. 1328, German Dominican preacher and speculative mystic, twenty-eight of whose propositions were condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329)
German Meister, master, his academic title; Eckhart from ecke, edge, and hart, hard. Eckhart von Hochheim.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Meister Eckhart was a Dominican provincial and a Paris master whose German sermons are among the most powerful ever preached in that language. His theme is the ground of the soul, a point at its centre where, he says, God and the soul meet without distinction; he speaks of an uncreated spark in man, of the birth of the Word in the soul, and of a detachment so complete that the soul wills nothing, not even God. Much of this is a straining after real things — union with Christ, the indwelling Spirit, self-denial — and his defenders argue that his daring language was pastoral paradox. But the propositions as they stand erase the line Scripture will not let be erased, between the Creator and the creature He made. Isa 42:8 is the boundary: “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another.” Act 17:28 grants the nearness — “For in him we live, and move, and have our being” — without any confusion of beings. Joh 1:12 gives the only sonship on offer: to those who received Him “gave he power to become the sons of God,” a becoming by adoption and grace, not an uncreated identity already there.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pantheism as the doctrine that the universe is God, or that all things are God; and mysticism as obscurity of doctrine.

expand to see more

PAN'THEISM, n. The doctrine that the universe is God, or the system of theology in which it is maintained that the universe is the supreme God.

PAN'THEIST, n. One that believes the universe to be God.

MYS'TICISM, n. Obscurity of doctrine. 2. The doctrine of the Mystics, who profess a pure, sublime and perfect devotion.

Key Scripture

Isa 42:8 — "I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images."

Act 17:28 — "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring."

Rom 1:25 — "Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen."

Joh 1:12 — "But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:"

Modern Corruption

Eckhart is the father of every spirituality that locates the divine in the depth of the self, and that is now the default religion of the educated West.

expand to see more

The uncreated ground of the soul is the seed of a vast modern harvest. Strip Eckhart of his Dominican vocabulary and what remains is the conviction that God is found by descending into the self, that the true self is divine, and that doctrine and ordinance are husks around that kernel. This is the common creed of therapeutic spirituality, of the perennialist account of all religions, and of a good deal of what is sold as contemplative Christianity. Rom 1:25 names the exchange it rests on: those “who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator.”

The recovery is the Creator-creature distinction held without apology, together with everything Scripture actually promises. The believer is united to Christ, indwelt by the Spirit, adopted as a son, conformed to the image of the Son and destined for glory — a nearness greater than Eckhart's and of a different kind, because it never stops being the nearness of two. Act 17:28 is as close as inspired language comes to his theme, and it is spoken of all men, pagans included, as a statement about dependence, not identity. God will not give His glory to another, and He does not need to, for He gives Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kabod (H3519), glory, weight; Greek ktisis (G2937), the creature, the thing created; teknon (G5043), a child.

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, honour, weight; Isaiah 42:8.

Hebrew shem (H8034) — name; Isaiah 42:8.

Greek ktisis (G2937) — creation, the creature; Romans 1:25.

Greek teknon (G5043) — a child, by birth or adoption; John 1:12.

Greek exousia (G1849) — right, authority; John 1:12.

Usage

"“my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8) — the line he blurred."

"“For in him we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28) — dependence, not identity."

"“gave he power to become the sons of God” (Joh 1:12) — sonship given, not innate."
